summary: The Internet Printing Protocol is an application-level protocol for distributed printing. This document, on the standards track as an internet standard, defines how IPP operations, attributes and values are encoded into the application/ipp media type and how those messages are carried over HTTP.

plainLanguage.summary: IPP lets computers talk to printers. This part says how the print requests are written down and sent over the web so printers understand them.

questions: how does ipp work over http
what is the internet printing protocol
what is the difference between ipp and ipps
subtitle: How IPP print requests are laid out as bytes in application/ipp and carried over HTTP to a printer.

tldr.problem: A print client and a printer need to agree on exactly how an operation such as printing a job is written as bytes, and how those bytes travel across the network.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8010 defines a binary format, the application/ipp media type, made of a version, an operation or status code, a request id, tagged attribute groups and optional document data. Every message is the body of an HTTP POST, by default on port 631.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 2910 and RFC 3382. The meaning of the operations and attributes lives in the companion Model and Semantics document, RFC 8011.

today: RFC 8010 is an Internet Standard published in January 2017. It obsoletes RFC 2910 and RFC 3382, and nothing is recorded as replacing or updating it. It is meant to be read together with RFC 8011.

sections.title: Two Layers: Operation and Transport
sections.content:
The Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) is an application-level protocol for distributed printing. RFC 8010 describes two layers. The transport layer is an HTTP request and response, and all IPP implementations support HTTP/1.1. The operation layer is the message body inside that request or response.

This RFC says how the operation layer is encoded and which HTTP rules apply. What the operations, attributes and values actually mean is defined by the IPP Model in RFC 8011 and its extensions. The words Client and Printer map to the HTTP user agent and HTTP server. A Printer represents one or more physical devices or a logical device, and it manages Job objects that each hold zero or more Document objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Printing over the network has two parts: the order form itself, and the envelope it travels in. This RFC explains how to fill in the form and which envelope to use.

sections.title: The IPP Message Layout
sections.content:
An operation request or response is a single message in the body of the HTTP request or response. It begins with a 2-byte version-number, then a 2-byte operation-id in a request or status-code in a response, then a 4-byte request-id whose value must be greater than 0. After that come zero or more attribute groups, a required one-byte end-of-attributes-tag, and optional data, such as the document to print.

Each group starts with a one-byte delimiter tag (for example 0x01 for operation attributes, 0x02 for job attributes, 0x04 for printer attributes and 0x05 for unsupported attributes). The end-of-attributes-tag is 0x03 and occurs exactly once. The Model, not this RFC, decides which groups appear and in what order for each operation.

The version-number of IPP/1.1 is a major byte of 1 and a minor byte of 1. If a Printer returns an IPP status-code, the HTTP status code MUST be 200 (OK). With any other HTTP status the response MUST NOT carry an IPP message body.
sections.plainLanguage: Every print message starts with the same boxes in the same order: which version, what you want done, a ticket number, then lists of details, and finally the document itself. A special marker says when the list of details is over.

sections.title: Attributes, Values and Tags
sections.content:
An attribute is a name plus one or more values. It is written as an attribute-with-one-value: a one-byte value-tag, a 2-byte name-length, the name, a 2-byte value-length and the value. Further values for the same attribute follow as additional-value fields, which look the same but have a name-length of zero. The zero-length name is the only mechanism for multi-valued attributes.

The value-tag says what type the value has. Examples are 0x21 for integer, 0x22 for boolean, 0x23 for enum, 0x44 for keyword, 0x45 for uri and 0x49 for mimeMediaType. Out-of-band tags such as 0x10 (unsupported), 0x12 (unknown) and 0x13 (no-value) carry a value-length of 0. Tag values from 0x00 to 0x0f are delimiters and 0x10 to 0xff are value tags.

All integers are signed, two's-complement, big-endian. They use 1 byte (SIGNED-BYTE), 2 bytes (SIGNED-SHORT) or 4 bytes (SIGNED-INTEGER). Integer and enum values are always exactly four octets and a boolean is one octet, 0x00 for false and 0x01 for true. A dateTime is eleven octets, a resolution is nine, and a rangeOfInteger is eight. Strings carry a charset and natural language, which the Model specifies. Text and name values with a language are built from length-prefixed pieces.

Collections group related member attributes. A collection starts with tag 0x34 (begCollection), holds member attributes introduced by the 0x4a memberAttrName tag, and ends with tag 0x37 (endCollection). This is the syntax that RFC 3382 used to define.
sections.plainLanguage: Each detail on the form is written as a label tag that says what kind of answer it is, how long the name is, the name, how long the answer is, and the answer. A second answer to the same question just leaves the name blank.

sections.title: Carrying IPP Over HTTP
sections.content:
HTTP/1.1 is the REQUIRED transport and HTTP/2 is OPTIONAL. Printers MUST support HTTP over the IANA-assigned well-known port 631, the IPP default port, and may also use other ports. Each HTTP operation MUST use the POST method, with the request-target set to the object the operation is aimed at and a Content-Type of application/ipp in both requests and responses.

An HTTP/1.1 server MUST support chunking for IPP requests, and an IPP Client MUST support chunking for IPP responses. A server may send a response before it has read the whole request, or an intermediate response such as 100 Continue, so Clients must expect that.

The target is named twice. The client must give it both as the HTTP request-target and as the operation attribute printer-uri or job-uri inside the body. The two may differ, for example a relative HTTP target and an absolute IPP URI, but they MUST refer to the same object, and the attribute URI MUST be absolute. The reason given is a consistent mapping of application/ipp onto transports that may not use URIs for addressing.
sections.plainLanguage: The print order goes inside an ordinary web request, sent to the printer's usual door, number 631. The address is written both on the envelope and on the form inside, and they must point at the same printer.

sections.title: ipp and ipps URIs
sections.content:
Printers and jobs are named with ipp URIs or secure ipps URIs. To send a request, the client converts the target to an HTTP URL by changing ipp to http (or ipps to https) and adding an explicit port 631 if none is present. The converted URL goes in the HTTP request line and headers, while the original ipp or ipps URI stays in the printer-uri or job-uri attribute in the body. A server uses the ipp or ipps form in the attributes of its responses.

For the example ipp://printer.example.com/ipp/print/myqueue, a direct request opens a TCP connection to port 631 and sends POST /ipp/print/myqueue HTTP/1.1. Through a proxy, the request line carries the full http://printer.example.com:631/... URL instead. A printer that registers itself with a directory service MUST register an ipp or ipps URI.
sections.plainLanguage: A printer's address starts with ipp in the print order, but on the web envelope it is rewritten to start with http and the door number 631 is added.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security requirements are set at a high level in RFC 8011: client authentication, server authentication and operation privacy. Clients and Printers SHOULD support HTTP Digest Authentication. The RFC explains that this is SHOULD rather than MUST because some low-end output devices have too little ROM space to justify it. Implementations that support Digest MUST support SHA2-256 and SHOULD support MD5 only for backward compatibility.

They SHOULD also support TLS for server authentication and operation privacy. TLS is not mandatory because earlier versions did not require it, but the RFC strongly encourages it since printing often involves sensitive documents. Basic Authentication SHOULD NOT be offered over insecure channels. Because printers often use self-signed certificates, clients SHOULD support Trust On First Use alongside normal certificate validation.

With ipp URIs, TLS is requested by the HTTP Upgrade mechanism. With ipps URIs, the TLS connection is negotiated immediately and unconditionally. A lower version-number in a request must never weaken security: a printer enforcing Digest Authentication for one version MUST do the same for version 1.1.
sections.plainLanguage: Print jobs can be private, so the best way is to use a locked tube between you and the printer. A tiny cheap printer may skip the lock, but the RFC says bigger ones should have it.

sections.title: Working With Other IPP Versions
sections.content:
The RFC does not require conformance to versions other than 1.1, but IPP was designed to make them easy. Printers SHOULD understand any valid request whose major version-number is greater than 0. They reply with the same version the client used if it is supported, or else the highest version they support. A client MUST send the highest version it supports and SHOULD retry with another version number after a server-error-version-not-supported error. Every IPP object MUST accept version 1.1 requests, unless it rejects them for some reason other than version support.

The target URI scheme in a request MUST match the scheme of one value of the printer's printer-uri-supported attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: Old and new printers can still talk. The client asks in the newest language it knows, and if the printer does not speak it, the client tries an older one.
